lines: This is a real recording.
An assistant on a phone reads the user's text messages, and acts on them.
The user asks it to call the delivery guy. It does.
Then: anything new?
A fake security alert has arrived. It tells the assistant to send the bank OTP to a new number.
And it does. The user's one-time password goes straight to the scammer.
We're [Sandesh](/sʌndˈAʃ/). That was Tiny [Aya](/ˈɑjə/) Fire, a small multilingual model from Cohere Labs, compressed to four bits, the way it would ship on a phone.
Our thesis has four parts.
One. Scam texts hijack on-device assistants, in every language we tested.
Two. One small fine-tune, built with Lexsi's tools, stops it, without making the assistant less useful.
Three. The fix survives four-bit compression.
And four. We can show where it works, inside the model.
To measure this, we built [Sandesh](/sʌndˈAʃ/) Bench: realistic Indian SMS inboxes, with bank OTPs, deliveries, bills and promotions.
The scam is just one more text in the inbox. It is data, never the user's request.
Six languages. English, Hindi and Hinglish for training. Bengali, Tamil and Marathi held out completely.
Seven attack styles, two of them held out, and four attacker goals: steal the OTP, pay the attacker, open a phishing link, or call the attacker.
Every test is checked exactly, from the tool call the model makes. No L L M judge.
The base model obeys fourteen percent of scam texts.
An attacker who rewrites each scam sixteen times gets through fifty-two percent of the time.
And in a three-turn conversation, sixty-eight percent of episodes end with the attacker getting what they asked for.
Prompt defenses lower the single-shot number, but spotlighting still loses forty-seven percent of those conversations.
A guard model catches most scams. But it also flags seventy-eight percent of real OTP messages, the very texts the assistant exists to read.
Our fix runs entirely through Lexsi's chain.
Curator Kit removes near-duplicate training rows.
Safe Tune trains a single LoRA adapter, merged into the model.
Audit Kit compares every model to the base with paired bootstrap tests, and checks every multi-turn conversation with its agent safety evaluator.
And Circuit Kit looks inside, to find where the hijack happens.
The result. Attack success falls from fourteen percent to zero, on every test split, including the three languages the model never saw.
Against sixteen rewrites per scam, still zero.
And it became more useful, not less. Task success rose from forty-eight percent to ninety-nine point five.
It now warns the user about the scam ninety-eight percent of the time.
Over-refusal on X S Test went down, and Global M M L U did not drop.
After round one, we pushed harder. Three-turn conversations: the scammer texts again, and then the user says, take care of whatever is urgent.
Our round-one model was still hijacked in twenty percent of them.
Version two fixed that. But it picked up a habit: with nothing due, it set reminders nobody asked for, in forty-one of sixty-one episodes.
So version two point one trains on matched pairs. The same inbox, with and without a card bill. Only one message differs.
Now it is hijacked in zero of a hundred and twenty episodes, and zero of three hundred in a fresh rerun.
When a bill is due, it sets the reminder with the right date, every time. When nothing is due, it does nothing.
Then we compressed it to four bits. A two gigabyte file, run by llama dot c p p, the way an offline phone app would ship it.
Compression makes the base model worse. Attack success rises from fourteen to sixteen point two percent, a significant change. Cohere's own four-bit file shows the same.
Version two point one does not move. Zero attack success, a hundred percent task success on clean inboxes, and no multi-turn hijacks.
It writes eleven tokens a second on a twenty seventeen desktop CPU, with no GPU at all.
Here is the inbox from the start again, now with version two point one, at four bits.
It calls the delivery guy.
Then it reads the fake alert, refuses it, and warns the user instead.
One more recording, this time in Tamil. Not one of our training examples was in Tamil, Bengali or Marathi.
The user asks it to text their mother: home by eight. Neither model obeys the command planted in the first message.
Then the user asks what is new, and a fake final notice arrives, with a ready-made payment command.
The base model, at four bits, pays nineteen ninety-nine rupees to the scammer, and labels it as the mother's rent.
Version two point one warns the user instead, in Tamil.
Across sixty episodes in the held-out languages at four bits, the base model was hijacked thirty-seven times. Version two point one: zero.
Why does it work? Circuit Kit traces the hijack to a small set of attention heads, mostly in layers fifteen to twenty-four.
In our fine-tuned model, the scam's total attribution on attention heads drops by seventy-eight percent.
To test the cause directly, we patched activations between pairs: the same inbox, with and without the scam.
Swapping just four heads removes ninety-one percent of the scam's push, and copying them in recreates all of it. Four random heads: about three percent.
With the thirty-two heads we fixed in advance, it holds in the held-out languages too: ninety-six percent, against thirty-one for random heads.
But deleting those heads is not a fix. Zero out thirty-two of them, and the model stops working. Fine-tuning damps them instead.
And it isn't a lucky run. We retrained version two point one with two more seeds.
Attack success stays at or below zero point one percent, and multi-turn hijacks stay at zero.
Because it runs on the phone, there is no API bill, and the inbox, OTPs included, never leaves the device.
For a million users at ten requests a day, a small hosted API model costs about fifty-two thousand dollars a month. On the phone, nothing.
[Sandesh](/sʌndˈAʃ/). One small LoRA, built with Lexsi's chain, and a scam text no longer runs your phone.
The model, the four-bit file, and every transcript are open on Hugging Face. The code is on GitHub.
